extracted.intended_audience: aspiring fiction writers and general writers (readers of Stephen King / craft-minded bloggers)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted guidance and practical craft rules from a blog review of Stephen King's On Writing: A Memoir of the Craft — advice aimed at fiction writers and general prose writers about process, style, and work habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with a 'Situation'
rubrics_metrics.description: Start a story with a situation — a tantalizing moment in ordinary life that in the author's imagination brims with menace and begs for development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: King noticed a stream and junk at a filling station and imagined slipping into water leading to escalating perversion (alien missing person, strange car). The situation should invite elaboration and move irresistibly to perversity and resolution; the situation is the seed from which the story develops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not organize a plot before writing / King dislikes plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Stephen King insists he doesn't like plots and does not pre-organize the plot before writing; instead the plot is the elaboration and resolution that emerges from the situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than planning out a plot, let the story develop by following the situation. Backstory and endings often emerge on their own as you write; King treats novel-writing sometimes like taking dictation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask 'What would real people do?' to develop scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: When developing the story, ask what the character or real people would do in the situation rather than forcing contrived actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This question drives authentic choices and keeps the narrative honest; it helps generate believable reactions, plot turns, and character revelations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let characters reveal themselves when the writing needs them
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters will show new aspects of their personalities at the point in the writing when the author needs to know about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to surprises from characters; sometimes events and character traits emerge mid-draft and change the direction of the work. King describes writing so fast at times that he scribbles to keep up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write first, revise later (revision is essential)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow the first draft to be more spontaneous (even unplanned) and then revise afterward to shape and improve the material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer tried King's approach for this post: typed without organizing ahead of time, then revised. The implication is that drafting freely then revising is an effective workflow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banish timidity; write courageously
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should banish timidity and write boldly rather than softening statements or providing escape-hatches to duck blame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King urges courageous writing — avoid hedging language that lets you avoid taking a stand. Example: prefer 'Bureaucrats criticize politicians...' over passive constructions that obscure agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dressing up vocabulary / use simple, appropriate words
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't hunt for long or pretentious words out of shame for short ones; use the first word that comes to mind if it is appropriate and colorful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pretentious word use is likened to dressing a pet in evening clothes — it embarrasses both pet and owner. Deciphering complicated words wastes reader time; prefer simplicity and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut unnecessary words
rubrics_metrics.description: Trim verbiage and tighten sentences by removing needless words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete tactics King recommends: 1) Use the possessive ('house's entrance' vs 'entrance of the house'); 2) Eliminate adverbs, which often weaken verbs; 3) Eliminate passive voice. These classic tactics shorten sentences and strengthen prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate adverbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Adverbs often weaken verbs and add unnecessary words; competent revision deletes many adverbs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King gives adverb-elimination as one of the chief ways to trim sentence size and strengthen verbs. The reviewer cites removing qualifiers like 'invariably' as unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid passive voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Passive voice dispenses with an explicit subject and can weaken a sentence by obscuring agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer active constructions that show who is doing what (example transformation given: 'Politicians who advocate for tax reductions will be criticized.' → 'Bureaucrats criticize politicians who advocate for tax reductions.'). Active voice is 'bolder' and clearer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read a lot and write a lot
rubrics_metrics.description: A core rule: read widely and write regularly; exposure to many books strengthens a writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King carries a book, recommends many titles (appendices of books he has read), and models indefatigable reading. The reviewer emphasizes carrying a book (kindle in pocket) and that this is 'standard issue' advice repeated by King.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a disciplined work ethic (daily practice, persistence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commit to disciplined, sustained writing (daily work, closed door, persistence through rejection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King's life demonstrates giftedness married to toil: he writes daily in an uninteresting room with the door closed, persisted through rejection letters, and treats writing as a vocation. Discipline and practice convert competent writers into good ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a trusted primary reader/critic
rubrics_metrics.description: Compose with a primary reader in mind who serves as the first critic (King's primary reader was his wife Tabatha).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King writes with Tabatha as his primary reader and gets a kick making her laugh at early drafts. Having a trusted early reader helps shape and test drafts before wider exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be honest and self-effacing in personal/memoir writing (avoid triumphalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing about personal struggles (e.g., addiction), adopt a self-effacing tone rather than triumphalist or self-congratulatory posture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King's account of addiction and recovery is modest; he credits his wife and presents recovery without boasting. This tone fosters sincerity and avoids alienating readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persist despite criticism; early work may be 'junk' but improves
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not be ashamed of early or criticized work; many published artists were accused of wasting talent yet improved through continued practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King's early mimeographed stories were called 'junk' yet he kept writing and publishing small works; criticism is common and shouldn't deter practice and publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow endings and backstory to emerge naturally
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of forcing an ending or backstory, allow these elements to present themselves during the writing process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer notes King lets endings and backstory emerge on their own as he writes, reinforcing the spontaneous/process-driven approach to narrative development.
